title: You shall gain your brother
theme: Christ makes reconciliation the aim of correction and gives his Church a patient, ordered path for seeking it. Private truth-telling, trustworthy witnesses, ecclesial judgment, binding and loosing, united prayer, and the Lord's own presence all serve the recovery of communion.
introduction: Jesus speaks neither of ignoring sin nor of exposing a brother at the first opportunity. He gives a discipline of charity. The person who has suffered wrong must first go privately, not to triumph over the offender but to gain him. Augustine insists that correction becomes Christian only when love seeks the wounded person's amendment; public disclosure of a private fault betrays rather than heals. If the first appeal fails, one or two witnesses join the work, and Chrysostom compares this patient escalation to a physician increasing the remedy when an illness does not yield. Only after repeated refusal is the matter brought to the Church. Even separation then does not erase concern for the person's salvation. Christ's teaching moves from the smallest encounter to the Church's authority because reconciliation is not merely private sentiment. The authority to bind and loose bears heavenly consequence and therefore demands justice. The promise given to agreed prayer likewise belongs to people gathered in ecclesial unity, asking what accords with Christ. At the passage's summit stands neither procedure nor human agreement by itself, but Jesus: wherever two or three gather in his name, he is already in their midst. Christian correction, judgment, prayer, and peace must all be measured by that presence.
hero_alt: Jesus teaches a small circle of disciples while two estranged brothers turn toward reconciliation, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and restrained luminous geometry
closing_title: Seek the brother, honor the Church, welcome Christ
closing: The Lord's sequence is demanding because it leaves little room for either avoidance or vengeance. Silence can disguise fear, comfort, or indifference; exposure can disguise wounded pride as zeal for truth. Jesus commands a harder mercy: go to the person, name the fault, and protect his dignity while seeking his return. If he will not listen, patience does not end. Others are invited so that truth may stand on reliable testimony and the work of healing may continue without becoming a private contest. The Church enters not as an audience for scandal but as the community entrusted with judgment, discipline, pardon, and the recovery of communion. Even when a person refuses her voice, Augustine warns that concern for his salvation remains. This passage therefore refuses easy oppositions between mercy and authority. Christ gives authority for the sake of restoration, and he ratifies just binding and loosing in heaven. He also promises that united prayer is not an attempt to bend God toward our grudges. Agreement must take shape in his name, within the peace and charity that make room for his presence. Before correcting someone, ask what you truly hope to gain. Is it vindication, an ally, an admission, or your brother? Before withdrawing, ask whether patient truth has been attempted. Before invoking community, ask whether you have protected the person's dignity and welcomed honest witnesses. Then pray together. Christ does not merely observe such faithful gathering from afar. He stands in its midst, making reconciliation a place of encounter with himself.

verses.text: But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he hears you, you shall gain your brother.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine says correction must be governed by love for the sinner, not self-love wounded by the offense. A private fault is addressed privately so that the brother may be healed without having his shame exposed.
verses.commentary: Augustine teaches that the purpose of rebuke is amendment, not the pleasure of finding blame or inflicting a wound. The offender has already injured himself by sin; to ignore that wound through indifference can be a further failure of charity. Yet love also protects his dignity. When only you know the fault, speak to him alone, because making a private sin public would betray rather than correct him. Forget the injury as your own grievance, Augustine says, but remember the spiritual harm suffered by your brother and seek to gain him back.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 18:15–17

verses.text: And if he will not hear you, take with you one or two more, so that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Chrysostom compares the widening circle of correction to a physician intensifying treatment when sickness persists. The witnesses support truth and healing; they are not recruited to overwhelm or humiliate.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom sees Christ's second step as evidence that correction seeks a cure rather than revenge. A physician does not abandon the sick when the first remedy fails, but applies greater care; likewise, the offended person should not turn from an unresponsive brother toward anger or hatred. Jesus does not begin with a crowd. Only after the private appeal fails does he command one or two others to come, fulfilling the law concerning witnesses. Their presence establishes what has been said and shows that every reasonable effort has been made for the brother's amendment.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 18:15–17

verses.text: And if he will not hear them, tell the Church. If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as the heathen and the publican.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine understands exclusion from the fellowship of brethren as real, but not as permission to abandon the sinner. The Church continues to desire his salvation just as she seeks the salvation of those still outside her visible communion.
verses.commentary: Augustine explains that one who refuses even the Church's correction is no longer to be regarded among the brethren. This judgment recognizes a rupture the person has stubbornly maintained; it does not pretend that communion survives unchanged when ecclesial admonition is rejected. Yet Augustine immediately limits any spirit of contempt. Christians do not count heathens among the brethren, but they still labor for their salvation. Thus discipline names separation truthfully while charity continues to hope and act for conversion. Even the final step remains ordered toward healing, not personal retaliation or permanent indifference.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 18:15–17

verses.text: Amen, I say to you: whatever you shall bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you shall loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.
verses.author: St Hilary of Poitiers
verses.insight: Hilary sees Christ placing solemn weight behind apostolic judgment. Binding leaves a person held in sin; loosing grants the pardon of God's mercy for salvation, and heaven ratifies this authority.
verses.commentary: Hilary reads this promise as a grave assurance that the apostles' judgment is not confined to earthly administration. What they bind—leaving a person entangled in the bond of sin—is bound in heaven; what they loose—granting the pardon of divine mercy for salvation—is loosed there as well. The authority is therefore both formidable and medicinal. It follows Christ's instructions for patient correction, testimony, and appeal to the Church, so it cannot be reduced to arbitrary power. Heaven's ratification gives ecclesial discipline its seriousness and directs its exercise toward repentance and saving mercy.
verses.source_label: St Hilary of Poitiers, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 18:18–20

verses.text: Again I say to you: if two of you consent upon earth concerning anything whatever they shall ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Chrysostom does not treat agreement as a formula that compels God. Those who pray together must live according to the Gospel, ask what is fitting, and refuse prayers shaped by vengeance.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom explains why apparent agreement does not always receive the thing requested. The petition may be harmful, the petitioners may fail to bring the obedient life Christ requires, or they may be seeking vengeance against those who grieved them. Christ's promise belongs to two who agree as people formed by the Gospel, not merely to two voices repeating the same desire. Read after the teaching on reconciliation, their prayer must share its purpose: truth, repentance, mercy, and restored communion. Genuine consent on earth is a harmony of life and intention beneath the Father's will.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 18:18–20

verses.text: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
verses.author: Origen
verses.insight: Origen lingers over Christ's present tense: he does not say that he will come later. As soon as believers truly agree in his name, Christ is found among them.
verses.commentary: Origen draws attention to the immediacy of Jesus' words. Christ does not promise, “I will be,” as though his presence followed after a delay; he says, “I am.” When believers come into genuine agreement, he is already in their midst. Origen also warns that disunity in doctrine and conduct disorders the Church's prayer like voices that fail to keep time in music. Gathering in Christ's name therefore means more than physical proximity. It is a concord shaped by his truth and way of life, within which the Lord makes his living presence known.
verses.source_label: Origen, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 18:18–20
